title: Kerala Families Await Return of Three Indians Killed in Germany Fire
excerpt: A Bochum building fire killed Sivin Johny, Nova Sabu and Anjali Sheela Joy, while a fellow resident was arrested and Kerala promised to cover repatriation through NORKA Roots.
body:
• Sivin Johny, 26, Nova Sabu, 25, and Anjali Sheela Joy, 27, all from Kerala, died in a fire early Tuesday in a residential building in Bochum, Germany.
  • German police have arrested a 41-year-old Romanian resident of the building on suspicion of murder, and investigators have ruled out a technical defect as the cause.
  • Five other residents were treated in hospital after inhaling smoke, as flames spread through the building's main stairwell.
  • Kerala will bear the repatriation costs through NORKA Roots, and the Indian Embassy in Berlin and the consulate in Frankfurt say they are assisting the families.

Three families in Kerala are waiting for the bodies of their children to be flown home from Germany, after a fire in a multi-family residential building in Bochum killed three young Indians who had moved abroad in recent months to study or find work.

The dead were identified in reporting by the Times of India as Sivin Johny, 26, of Kalady in Ernakulam district, Nova Sabu, 25, of Kattappana in Idukki district, and Anjali Sheela Joy, 27, of Chemmakkad in Kollam district.

What happened in Bochum

The fire broke out at about 4.15 a.m. local time on Tuesday in the Hofstede district of Bochum, according to The Indian Eye, citing German media and police. Firefighters found the three victims dead inside an apartment on the building's second floor. Flames spreading up the main stairwell made the rescue harder, forcing crews to reach other residents by ladders and a safety cushion.

Five other residents suffered severe smoke inhalation and were taken to hospitals in Bochum. Their nationalities have not been confirmed.

Police and prosecutors announced on Wednesday that a 41-year-old Romanian national who lived in the building had been arrested on strong suspicion of murder after questioning by a homicide squad. Investigators have ruled out a technical defect and suspect arson, but they are still examining whether the fire was set deliberately or started accidentally during a conflict. The official causes of the three deaths have not been confirmed.

Three short stays in Germany

Relatives gave reporters a picture of three arrivals with plans still taking shape. Johny travelled to Germany last month in search of employment and was expected to start a job this week, a relative said. His brother, Salvin, is studying nursing in Germany.

Joy travelled in July to look for a teaching job and was working in a warehouse while she searched for work in education, her uncle said. Sabu also moved in July, to pursue studies, and was working part time as a gym trainer, according to her relatives. Her father is a retired police officer and her mother works at a public health centre in Idukki district.

Families learned of the deaths through relatives, friends and Malayali contacts in Germany before formal paperwork was complete. They are now in touch with those contacts while the procedures for release and transport of the bodies are completed.

Repatriation effort

Kerala's government said on Thursday that it is coordinating with India's Ministry of External Affairs, the Indian Embassy in Germany and Malayali associations to bring the remains home at the earliest, and that the state, through NORKA Roots, would bear all expenses related to repatriation. That commitment removes the transport cost from the three families; the remaining wait is for German formalities to be completed.

Members of Parliament and state legislators have approached the external affairs ministry seeking faster procedures. Lok Sabha MP Benny Behanan visited Johny's home in Kalady on Thursday, met his parents, and said he was in touch with the German Embassy and contacts in Germany.

The Indian Embassy in Berlin and the Consulate General of India in Frankfurt said they are in contact with local authorities and the bereaved families and are providing assistance. German authorities continue to investigate the fire.

What happens next

No date for the arrival of the bodies in Kerala has been announced. That timing depends on the German investigation, identification and release formalities, and flight arrangements coordinated by the embassy and NORKA Roots. For the families in Kalady, Kattappana and Chemmakkad, the priority stated in every account is the same: bringing their loved ones home so last rites can be performed in Kerala.
